about: Property-based tests and fuzzing of Kolaboro's open scoring rules. Generated by the open-source repository CI; every number below is counted by the test run itself.
runner: local run of the repository CI steps (the repository is not public yet)

properties.property: score and confirmed score stay between 0 and 6, tier is one of caution, mixed, clear
confirming a check (registry or independent source) never lowers the score, the confirmed score or the tier, and adds at most one confirmed point
publishing one more check never lowers the score or the tier; crossing into public adds exactly one point
the score is exactly the number of public checks, one point per check
a problem in public reports never raises the tier and never changes the score; any flag means caution
with the same reports and research depth, a higher score never gives a lower tier
same input, same output: repeated calls, reordered keys and copies give identical results, and inputs are not modified
every researcher note maps to exactly one known verification level
a public report of guaranteed returns can only remove the no-guaranteed-returns point, never add one
months overdue is never negative, is empty for completed projects, and never decreases as time passes
the market transparency index is between 0 and 100, needs 3 or more projects, and never falls when one project publishes or confirms more
score, confirmed score and tier equal an independent restatement of the published rules (only registry and independent sources confirm)
months overdue equals whole months after the end of the promised period (year: December, quarter: its last month), for projects not completed
the transparency index equals 60% average score/6 + 30% average confirmed/6 + 10% share without public problems, within 0.05 rounding

every "what would change this score" answer is consistent: publishing one check adds exactly one point, confirming one adds at most one confirmed point
JavaScript (p/whatif.js) and Python (open/scoring.py) give the same score, confirmed score, tier and verification levels on random inputs
the market transparency index in JavaScript (ti-core.js) and Python (open/scoring.py) agree to one decimal
